content.body:
Why women stop losing weight on a GLP-1

I'm a nurse practitioner, and most of my patients are on a GLP-1 now.

Somewhere around month three or four I start hearing the same question, almost word for word. "I was losing every week and now nothing. Did it stop working?"

Usually no. The medication is doing what it always did.

And plateaus are normal, most people hit one at some point.

But some run way longer than they should. And when one drags past a couple of months, in my care the most common reason is elevated cortisol.

Think about what your body is actually dealing with in those first months.

You're eating a lot less than it's used to. A sustained calorie deficit raises cortisol, that part is just physiology.

Many people get nausea on top, some of them daily. Plus constipation, headaches, fatigue.

Sleep gets worse for a lot of my patients too. They wake more often and get less rest out of the same hours.

Each of those raises cortisol a little further. And there's even research suggesting the shot itself raises it, which is why upping the dose often buys you a longer plateau instead of a shorter one.

Here's why that matters for your weight.

High cortisol slows your metabolism down. Your body shifts from burning fat to holding on to it, and it pulls energy out of muscle first because muscle is expensive to keep.

That's also the window where hair shedding tends to show up.

So the GLP-1 pulls one way and cortisol pulls the other. And you sit at the same weight for eight, ten, twelve weeks while doing everything right.

I've had patients in that spot eating well, walking every day, never missing a dose. They weren't failing, their cortisol was high, and nobody had checked it.

Nobody checks it, by the way. Cortisol isn't on any standard GLP-1 panel, and most endocrinologists only run it if they suspect Cushing's.

You can't out-discipline a stress response. If cortisol is what's holding your weight, the fix is lowering the cortisol, not trying harder.

I don't think that applies to everyone who stalls. But if you're past month two with hair shedding, low energy, disrupted sleep, muscle loss, food noise creeping back, slower weight loss, cortisol is where I'd look first.

There's decent research on lowering it naturally, alongside the shot rather than instead of it.

The two compounds with the strongest evidence are saffron extract and gingerol-standardized ginger extract.

Saffron is the one with actual cortisol data. It's been studied for cortisol regulation, mood, and the sleep piece, which covers most of the stress inputs above.

Ginger works on the gut, where most GLP-1 side effects live. Less nausea means one less thing your system reads as stress.

Together they sit on the loop that keeps a plateau going. The side effects stress the body, the stress raises cortisol, and the cortisol holds the weight.

They can help break that loop so the shot can keep doing its job. But only if your cortisol is actually high.

One of my patients was stuck for six weeks before we tried it. Two weeks in she was losing again, and she's down another 19 pounds since.

I'm not promising that timeline to anyone, and none of this is magic.

But if your weight has been stuck for months and you've been blaming your discipline, it's probably not your discipline.

If you're on a GLP-1 and stalled, or losing hair and muscle while you wait it out, this is where I'd start.
